S1.01.displayTitle: Binary and decimal prefixes use different scales

steps.label: Read
steps.title: Look for the i
steps.detail: Ki, Mi, Gi and Ti signal the binary scale.

steps.label: Choose
steps.title: Select 1024 or 1000
steps.detail: Binary prefixes climb by 1024; decimal prefixes climb by 1000.

steps.label: Label
steps.title: Keep the unit exact
steps.detail: KiB and kB are not interchangeable labels.

cue.title: Two staircases
cue.text: A binary staircase has 1024 steps per level; a decimal staircase has 1000. The labels tell you which staircase to climb.

S1.02.displayTitle: Bases and signed representations answer different questions

steps.label: Classify
steps.title: Base or representation?
steps.detail: Binary, denary and hex are bases; BCD and complements encode values.

steps.label: Fix
steps.title: Keep the bit width
steps.detail: Signed representations only make sense when every value uses the stated width.

steps.label: Interpret
steps.title: Apply the stated rule
steps.detail: The same bits can mean a different value under a different representation.

cue.title: One value, several name tags
cue.text: +23 is 00010111 in 8-bit binary; the rules create different 8-bit patterns for -23.

S1.03.displayTitle: Choose the conversion method from the target

steps.label: Target
steps.title: Name the destination
steps.detail: Write the required base or representation before starting.

steps.label: Method
steps.title: Use its shortest route
steps.detail: Use place values, four-bit groups or digit-by-digit BCD.

steps.label: Check
steps.title: Convert back
steps.detail: Reverse the method and confirm the value and bit width.

cue.title: 45 takes different forms
cue.text: 45 denary is 00101101 binary, 2D hexadecimal and 0100 0101 in BCD.

S1.04.displayTitle: Signed arithmetic keeps one fixed-width bit pattern

steps.label: Encode
steps.title: Prepare both operands
steps.detail: Use the same width and encode a negative operand correctly.

steps.label: Operate
steps.title: Add column by column
steps.detail: Subtraction can be performed by adding the two's-complement negative.

steps.label: Interpret
steps.title: Keep the stored width
steps.detail: Discard only a carry beyond the fixed width, then decode the result.

cue.title: A four-bit number line
cue.text: 0101 + 1101 represents 5 + (-3). The stored four-bit result is 0010, which represents 2.

S1.05.displayTitle: Overflow means the true result does not fit

steps.label: Range
steps.title: Find representable limits
steps.detail: Use both the bit width and the stated signed representation.

steps.label: Calculate
steps.title: Find the true result
steps.detail: Do the arithmetic without assuming every carry means overflow.

steps.label: Decide
steps.title: Compare result with range
steps.detail: Overflow occurs only when the true result lies outside the limits.

cue.title: A box with fixed capacity
cue.text: Eight-bit two's complement ends at 127. Therefore 127 + 1 overflows even though an 8-bit pattern is still stored.

S1.06.displayTitle: BCD and hexadecimal suit different real uses

steps.label: Need
steps.title: Identify the practical task
steps.detail: Ask whether exact decimal digits or compact binary notation matters.

steps.label: Choose
steps.title: Match the representation
steps.detail: Use BCD for digit displays and hex for compact bit patterns.

steps.label: Justify
steps.title: State why it fits
steps.detail: Connect the representation's structure directly to the application.

cue.title: Display versus shorthand
cue.text: A clock stores 59 as BCD 0101 1001. A debugger writes 1101 0110 compactly as D6.

S1.07.displayTitle: Character sets map symbols to binary codes

steps.label: Map
steps.title: Character becomes a number
steps.detail: The character set defines the numeric code for each symbol.

steps.label: Store
steps.title: Code becomes bits
steps.detail: The numeric code is represented internally in binary.

steps.label: Choose
steps.title: Match the needed range
steps.detail: Unicode is suitable when many languages and symbols are required.

cue.title: A numbered library catalogue
cue.text: The computer stores a catalogue number, not the drawn symbol. The character set tells it which symbol that number means.

S1.08.displayTitle: A bitmap stores metadata plus a grid of pixels

steps.label: Count
steps.title: Find the number of pixels
steps.detail: Multiply image width by image height.

steps.label: Encode
steps.title: Apply bits per pixel
steps.detail: Multiply the pixel count by colour depth.

steps.label: Convert
steps.title: Change bits to bytes
steps.detail: Divide by 8 and add a header only when instructed.

cue.title: A mosaic with a label card
cue.text: The pixel grid is the mosaic; the header is the label card. A 100 × 80 image at 8 bits per pixel uses 64,000 pixel-data bits.

S1.09.displayTitle: A vector file stores drawing instructions

steps.label: Store
steps.title: Save objects and properties
steps.detail: The file records how each object should be drawn.

steps.label: Render
steps.title: Follow the drawing list
steps.detail: Software redraws the objects at the requested size.

steps.label: Choose
steps.title: Match image to task
steps.detail: Use vectors for scalable shapes and bitmaps for pixel-level detail.

cue.title: Recipe versus mosaic
cue.text: A vector logo is a recipe that can be cooked at any size; a bitmap photograph is a fixed mosaic of sampled colours.

S1.10.displayTitle: Sampling measures a wave at discrete moments

steps.label: Time
steps.title: Measure the wave repeatedly
steps.detail: Sampling rate controls how often amplitude is measured.

steps.label: Level
steps.title: Encode each measurement
steps.detail: Sampling resolution controls the available amplitude levels.

steps.label: Trade-off
steps.title: Balance accuracy and size
steps.detail: Higher rate or resolution improves approximation but stores more data.

cue.title: Graph paper for sound
cue.text: Sampling rate adds more columns in time; sampling resolution adds more rows for amplitude. A finer grid follows the wave more closely.

S1.11.displayTitle: Compression removes or rewrites repeated information

steps.label: Inspect
steps.title: Find repeated or removable data
steps.detail: Different file types contain different kinds of redundancy.

steps.label: Choose
steps.title: Decide whether exactness matters
steps.detail: Use lossless when every original bit must be reconstructed.

steps.label: Justify
steps.title: Connect method to application
steps.detail: State the size benefit and the acceptable quality consequence.

cue.title: Packing versus trimming
cue.text: RLE packs AAAABB as 4A2B without losing data. Lossy media compression trims detail that the chosen application can tolerate.
